# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Clinical Review

## Introduction
For decades, transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (TV-ICDs) have served as the cornerstone for preventing sudden cardiac death (SCD). However, the presence of transvenous leads introduces substantial long-term vulnerabilities, including lead fracture, venous thrombosis, systemic infection, and tricuspid valve dysfunction. To bypass these intravascular complications, the entirely subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed and subsequently approved for clinical use after landmark feasibility studies [1]. By positioning both the pulse generator and the electrode subcutaneously in the left lateral thoracic and parasternal regions, the S-ICD protects patients from catastrophic lead-related intravascular complications.

## Patient Selection and Pre-Implant Screening
Selecting appropriate candidates for S-ICD therapy requires balancing the prevention of SCD against the S-ICD's lack of chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), and anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP). Current European and American guidelines recommend the S-ICD for patients who have an indication for an ICD but do not require pacing therapy, particularly those with difficult vascular access, a high risk of device-related infection, or a long life expectancy where lead preservation is paramount [3, 4].

A key step in patient selection is electrocardiographic (ECG) screening to evaluate QRS-T morphology [2]. Because the S-ICD relies on far-field subcutaneous signals, it is susceptible to T-wave oversensing (TWO), which can result in inappropriate shocks. Patients must pass screening in at least one vector (supine and standing) using manual template tools or automated screening software to ensure the device can reliably differentiate cardiac depolarizations from repolarizations [12]. S-ICD therapy has proven highly successful in young patients and those with channelopathies, such as Brugada syndrome, where pacing is rarely required [16, 17].

## Clinical Trials and Real-World Evidence
The clinical efficacy of the S-ICD was first established in the United States Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) trial [7] and further validated in the real-world EFFORTLESS registry [5, 6]. A pooled analysis of these early trials demonstrated excellent shock efficacy and low complication rates [8]. The long-term safety and efficacy profile of the S-ICD was directly compared to the TV-ICD in the PRAETORIAN trial [9]. This randomized, head-to-head clinical trial met its primary endpoint, demonstrating that the S-ICD was non-inferior to the TV-ICD regarding a composite endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [9]. Additionally, long-term registry data have repeatedly confirmed the durability and clinical performance of the S-ICD in diverse real-world cohorts [27].

## Mitigating Inappropriate Shocks
Historically, inappropriate shocks due to supraventricular tachycardias or T-wave oversensing were a major limitation of subcutaneous defibrillators [11]. Significant technical iterations have dramatically reduced these events. The development of dual-zone programming (conditional and shock zones) [19] and the introduction of the SMART Pass sensing filter [14] have drastically minimized inappropriate therapies. The SMART Pass filter attenuates lower-frequency signals like T-waves without compromising ventricular fibrillation detection [13, 15]. The prospective UNTOUCHED trial evaluated contemporary S-ICD programming (high-rate cutoffs and active SMART Pass filtering) in primary prevention patients with reduced ejection fractions [10]. The trial demonstrated an exceptionally low inappropriate shock rate of 3.1% at one year, proving that modern S-ICD programming achieves rates comparable to or better than those of modern TV-ICDs [10].

## Procedural Optimization and Future Directions
Implantation techniques have evolved from the original three-incision technique to a streamlined two-incision approach, which improves cosmetic outcomes and shortens procedure times. Postoperative pain management has also improved; the use of regional anesthesia, specifically the serratus anterior plane block (SAPB), has significantly reduced post-procedural opioid consumption and facilitated same-day discharges [20, 21]. Furthermore, intraoperative defibrillation testing (DFT), which was historically mandatory, is increasingly omitted. Instead, clinicians utilize the PRAETORIAN score, an anatomical tool based on chest radiography, to predict the likelihood of successful defibrillation based on generator and lead positioning [22, 23].

If systemic infections do occur, extracting an S-ICD is far less risky than extracting a transvenous lead, as it avoids intravascular traction [18, 28]. This clinical advantage makes the S-ICD a highly attractive option in younger patients, offering superior lifetime cost-effectiveness despite higher initial device costs [29, 30]. Finally, to address the limitation of S-ICD's lack of pacing capability, modular systems co-implanting the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker (LP) have been successfully evaluated [24, 25]. These systems communicate wirelessly, allowing the LP to deliver ATP for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, effectively expanding S-ICD candidacy to patients requiring pacing [26].
